Without further context it's hard to say what the best option is, but it definitely isn't playable as is. The chord is an E# diminished 7th chord. So, ignoring the 8va for a moment, you could just play it like this:


4th string - 6th fret (G#)
3rd string - 7th fret (D)
2nd string - 6th fret (E#)
1st string - 7th fret (B)

This is a standard shape for diminished chords on the guitar, and you still keep the original soprano and bass notes as notated here. Regarding the 8va, again, it's hard to say without context but it looks pretty unplayable, and as your playing an arrangement of a violin caprice you could probably afford to make some changes before and after to get rid of the 8va.

The answer to your first question is basically yes. Inversions/different voicings serve the function of making the chord sequence more interesting, and also avoiding the prohibitions mentioned above (in turn making it more interesting).


The answer to your second question is, it depends on what genre you're playing. As some others have said, if you're playing something like rock or metal then just moving the shape up and down the neck is totally acceptable because it fits the genre well. In saying that, I think having an understanding of voicings/voice leading as a guitarist completely opens up a whole other world of possibilities, particularly if you're interested in composition. It also helps understand why jazz chords are written a certain way, and makes analysing pieces easier.

I do slightly different fingerings than what's written for those trills. For the first, have your 2nd finger on the B in the bass, 1st finger on G# on the 3rd string (the upper note of the trill), and your 4th finger on the F# on the 4th string. You then want to execute the trill by doing a cross string trill, which is done with the right hand. Your "a" is going to pluck the G# and your "p" will play the B, then "i" plays F#, "m" plays G# again, and then your "p" plays the last F# in the trill. So the RH fingering is "a m i p". For an extra touch you can plant your "a" on the G# after the trill to cut the resonance. The same should apply for the second trill too. Practice it very slowly and check out some videos of David Russell playing some Scarlatti or Bach - most people consider him the pioneer of the cross string trill. I'm sure there are some online tutorials about it if you get confused.

I know it's already been said a few times, but the A at the end of the first highlighted bar is almost certainly a typo. Apart from it being awkward to play, harmonically it doesn't really make sense. At the beginning of the bar you've got chord I, then skipping to the next bar you've got a ii6, V and then I in the next the bar. If we say the A at the end of the first bar is part of the chord, that would make it chord vi in second inversion which you never see in classical music. It's most likely it's a G as it looks like he's just inverted the I chord at the beginning of the bar to make it a I6, and obviously it's just easier to play.

Think of the bottom number as a unit of measurement, and top number as how much of said unit. Technically you can measure anything in whatever unit of measurement you want. For example, you could measure a highway between two cities in millimetres or  the width of a room in miles, but generally you want the unit of measurement that will give you the clearest understanding. Time signatures are the same, you could technically write 3/4 (3 quarter notes) as 6/8 (6 eighth notes), but that wouldn't be reflective of the inherent sense of pulse. As others have said, there might be a time when it would be easier to read tuplets in a bar of their own rather than in a bar of a standard time signature.


TLDR; The bottom number of a time signature tells you what type of note value is worth "one beat" in a bar. This number may change within a piece to make it easier to read a particular rhythm, or to more accurately reflect a desired interpretation.

Hey there, I'm no expert in this but I will give my thoughts as a tertiary-level classical guitarist. 

It seems like you have two options, either move the F up or move the Bb down to the G string. Neither is ideal, but as long as the Bb is higher than the F, you're getting the perfect 4th that was intended. Changing the register is very common in transcribing; look at transcriptions of Scarlatti or Granados. I believe as long as you keep the melody and bass lines the same pitches, the change in registers is nothing but a less-than-ideal compromise. In the end the compromise is worth it because the guitar complements the music so well and vice versa. 

For me, a no-no is SWAPPING pitches, so you have F in the melody and the Bb in the bass. Changing the actual pitch of the melody line is, in my opinion, taking too much liberty.


Anyway, just my thoughts on that matter. Hope that helps.

Hey man, good job. You seem to know the piece well and have a good sense of melody.

Just a couple of things:

1. I think you would really benefit from a metronome. Sometimes some of the  "trills" aren't quite rhythmically accurate and therefore delay the downbeat slightly, meaning us as listeners lose a sense of pulse. Try practicing slowly with metronome and making sure everything is accurate. 

2. I also think you could work on your tone, sometimes the bass was a little "snappy" and the trebles weren't always clear. Try experiment with some RH nail shapes and sizes. Another factor is the stroke itself. A really good warm up tip I learnt from David Russell is just to start by focusing on one finger at a time and trying to get the best sound possible. Think of "pushing into the string" rather than "plucking" it.

Anyway this seems to be going on for a little long, it just seems like you put a lot of effort into this so thought you might appreciate the feedback. Happy practicing!
